utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Just a reminder that we are again sitting under the provisions of Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Kwon. Good morning, Mr. Neskovic. Could you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would like to sit down and make yourself comfortable, and then Mr. Tieger will commence the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Krajisnik on the 18th, 19th, and 20th of July, 2005; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you've had the opportunity to review the audio tapes of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you confirm for the Trial Chamber, then, that your testimony accurately reflected your statements before the Court and that if examined on the same subjects in this court, that the information you would provide would be the same; in short, that you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Basically yes, although some words would be different. I would not be able to repeat everything in the same words every time again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think a verbatim memory quiz is what the rule had in mind, Mr. Neskovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, P22217, the entirety of the testimony from the Krajisnik case from 18 July through 20 July 2005, is now tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2568, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I will proceed to read the summary or address the associated exhibits as the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, if you just read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Radomir Neskovic, a public -- well, let me explain for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'll be reading for the Court a short summary of your testimony. It's not intended to capture all the details and is not intended to replace your evidence which is, in fact, in evidence. It's just intended as a guide so that the evidence is briefly summarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radomir Neskovic, a public opinion researcher by profession, was asked by Mr. Karadzic in August 1990 to join the SDS, to do research and analysis of public opinion for the party and he attended meetings of the Main Board. On 12 July 1991, Mr. Neskovic was on a list of names proposed by Dr. Karadzic for the Main Board and was elected to be a member of the SDS Main Board. He was elected deputy chairman of the SDS Executive Board on or around 31 July 1991. In 1992, the witness was also President of the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo. In 1993, he considered himself to be a de facto member of the Executive Board of the SDS. The SDS party was hierarchical and once a decision was taken, it was necessary for this decision to be implemented by all the bodies - by the local board, by the municipal boards. Each member of the local committee would be active on behalf of about 20 households. Obedience was required and municipal bodies could be dismissed if they failed to implement the party's policies. Mr. Karadzic was the undisputed authority in the party and expected obedience. After joining the SDS, Mr. Neskovic visited many municipalities to resolve organisational and staff issues and conflicts. He was tasked to do so by either the SDS Executive Board or Main Board or directly from Mr. Karadzic. Upon return, he would submit a report to the Executive Board or to Mr. Karadzic personally, although he came to realise that Karadzic was already informed of what he had been involved in even before he had returned from the field. In addition to emissaries such as Mr. Neskovic, Dr. Karadzic communicated with the municipal leadership of the SDS in various ways, including direct contact with municipal leaders by phone and fax and letters. In addition, leaders from municipalities very frequently came to see Mr. Karadzic for various questions and issues. Mr. Karadzic could authorise these municipal officials to act and they would do so accordingly. As a member of the Main Board and Executive Board, Mr. Neskovic was present at a meeting of a large number of SDS functionaries held in the Holiday Inn around 19 December 1991. Mr. Neskovic testified that at this gathering Mr. Karadzic distributed numbered copies of the Variant A and B document to municipal representatives. Mr. Karadzic gave an introductory speech that had to do with the threat that Serbs were under and then municipal leaders were called up to take the document and told to read it. He understood that it was mandatory for those who received the A and B document, that is, persons who held high-ranking positions within the local authorities, to implement the document, although it was up to them to decide how best to do so. The witness also testified about the implementation of Variants A and B instructions in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, where he was a member of the Crisis Staff set up pursuant to those instructions. Mr. Karadzic devoted much attention to those holding formal positions on behalf of the SDS in the governmental authorities, such as members of the Presidency, Serb ministers, president of the Assembly, and MUP representatives and would "focus on his representatives within the organs of power." Many persons appointed to high-level positions were personal picks of Mr. Karadzic, including the president of the Assembly, Mr. Karadzic's close associate Momcilo Krajisnik. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik often visited party bodies when it came to personnel policies and they would appoint individuals to posts in executive power structures. The personnel in the Ministry of Interior in the MUP were also personally chosen by Mr. Karadzic. The witness also testified that Muslims were expelled in droves from Grbavica and also testified about a man named Batko who maltreated and terrorised people and whose main targets were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I have a few additional questions for you, but as I advised the Trial Chamber, my examination-in-chief will be brief. First of all, Mr. Neskovic, although it's alluded to in your testimony, I don't think it's explicit, can you tell the Court for how long you continued to be a member of SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the SDS beginning with 12 July 1990 until August 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted also to ask you about an issue that may be related to two aspects of your testimony. Your evidence was that the SDS party was hierarchical, that it was necessary for decisions from the top to be implemented by the lower bodies, and that members could be dismissed if they failed to implement party policies. And you also testified that at the meeting in December at the Holiday Inn at which the Variant A and B document was disseminated, that the atmosphere was emotionally charged and that it was not conducive to discussion about the substance of the document because one might have appeared to be a traitor if one appeared to be rejecting the document. Now, I wanted first to ask what was the significance during those times of being labelled or called a traitor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stated that, thinking that it might happen that way; however, at that meeting it didn't happen and nobody even discussed the document. It was just an assumption on my part. If somebody were to be called a traitor, that person would lose their reputation among the Serbs, among their acquaintances, among the party members. That would mean losing one's standing and one's influence in the Serbian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did concerns about the consequences of being deemed a traitor also play a role in general party discipline?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Party discipline applied to the implementation of policy. A person who would fail to implement the party policy or would cause conflicts at the level of lower organs of the SDS would be sanctioned for that failure. If somebody were labelled a traitor in the Serbian community would not necessarily entail disciplining on the part of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you testified that members of the Main Board would regularly attend meetings of municipal boards in the areas they were from and that this was one of the ways that SDS policies were communicated to and followed by those in the field. Did the SDS deputies, first those in the joint Assembly and then later in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, play a role in conveying information to the field and relaying to the leadership what was happening in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about deputies. I don't have that information. But it certainly applied to members of the Main Board. Members of the Main Board regularly attended meetings of municipal boards in their native places, and the relationship between grass-roots organisations of the SDS and the leadership of the party was very strong, very well developed. There were many contacts from the top down and vice versa. Speaking of members of the Main Board, the answer is yes; but as far as members of the parliament are concerned, I'm not sure to what extent they were involved in municipal organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified that part of the organisational structure to facilitate communications was that each member of a local board was to be active on behalf of 20 households. And just to be clear, were those local board members expected to report the information they received directly to the SDS leadership at the central level or to the municipal boards immediately above them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The basic organisation was the local board, that's the lowest organisation of the SDS, and it would have up to 15 members. Each of the members was in charge of some 15 to 20 households where he represented the SDS, and he would inform the local board, the local board would inform the municipal board, and the municipal board would report to the president of the party or the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neskovic, you explained to the Court in 2005 that when you returned from the field, you would report back to either the Main Board or the Executive Board or to Mr. Karadzic himself, and if you wanted to submit a report to Mr. Karadzic, you realised that he was already informed of what you had been involved in even before you returned. I wanted to ask you how you came to this realisation, whether it was from discussions directly with Dr. Karadzic, from others in the SDS. How did you come to realise that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I usually reported to Mr. Karadzic verbally concerning the work I had done in a particular municipality, but he never insisted on an exhaustive verbal report. Our conversations would be very short, from which I concluded that he had already received reports from the municipal board or somebody else in the municipality. So he was informed already, and that's why he did not ask me for an exhaustive report. That's how I made that inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you went to the field, did local leaders speak to you about or provide you with information about their contact with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you came to address the issues that you had to address and focused on those issues with them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I always asked that they specify what I'm supposed to do. It was usually about conflicts between different factions within the organisation and I played the role of mediator to defuse those tensions. That's what I usually dealt with, not other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Neskovic, you testified that Mr. Karadzic was the undisputed authority in the SDS party and that he, along with Mr. Krajisnik, was the supreme authority of the Serb movement, whose policies were implemented through deputies, ministers, MUP officials, through people in government, whether it was the joint government of BiH or later in Republika Srpska. And although you seemed to put a start date on that situation by reference to the time when there was still a joint government, I wanted to ask you for how long this was the case, that is, was that the case during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That concludes the examination-in-chief. With respect to the associated exhibits, I advised the Court yesterday about one issue. I don't believe there's any -- and that is the incorrect listing of 65 ter 01482 on the list of documents to be used rather than the associated exhibits. I also note that the second-to-last reference in the listing of associated exhibits, that is 00332 should be 06079, those are two documents of the same date bearing on the same issue, but it is 06079 that is referred to at transcript page 16834. I've spoken with Mr. Robinson about that and he has no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't object to any of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. While you're on your feet, Mr. Robinson, it's a collateral issue. The Prosecution has put in a motion with respect to the recommencement of the evidence of Dr. Treanor. Would you -- could you be in a position to respond to that orally at some point this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I can do that right now. I don't think we would have any objection to that. We have also today sent a letter to the Prosecution asking for disclosure of the other interviews at which Mr. Treanor was present, so that we can see whether there was any other material that hasn't been disclosed to us that could be relevant to his cross-examination. But assuming there is none, I don't see any reason why we couldn't go ahead with his testimony after this witness concludes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that sufficient for your purposes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I haven't had an opportunity to see the letter, but it sounds like we'll be moving forward and that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it's now your opportunity to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Neskovic. Has anyone heard me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, you're coming through my microphone -- earphones certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Neskovic. I don't know if you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. I heard. I heard the second part. I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you, you were kind enough to meet with my advisor on the 10th of October, 2009, and on that occasion a transcript was made of that interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must ask you that both of us make a pause between questions and answers so we don't overlap and make things hard for the interpreters. Has my advisor sent you a transcript of that interview for your consideration?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you answer the same questions today in the same way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Basically yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us start from the beginning. You described our meeting and the moment you joined the Serbian Democratic Party. Do we agree that before the 12th of July, 1990, the two of us did not know each other and we met the night before the day when the SDS was established?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that you with your democratic party of freedom that had already been established as well as other parties and movements collectively joined the SDS at that session of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, knowing about your career record, did I ask you to take charge of analytical affairs in the party, especially analysing the public opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in August 1990 in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you became deputy, or rather, vice-president of the Executive Board or deputy president of the Executive Board, and at the next electoral assembly you became member of the Main Board too?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I attended the Main Board meeting at Ilidza from August 1990, and I believe I was co-opted by you onto the Main Board. However, I became member of the Executive Board at the elections on the 31st of July, 1991, after the electoral assembly held on the 12th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that your memory is better than mine. Now, do you remember that one of the main initiators in the formation of the Serbian Democratic Party was Mr. Aleksandar Vukovic, a political scientist, a specialist lawyer and so on and so forth. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean Aca from Grbavica, the old Aca, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's the same person. Now, I'd like to show you a document which is connected with our cadres election.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we have 1D3558 on our screens on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have here the two versions, both in Serbian and in English. Let me remind you that on the 12th of January, 1991, which is to say right after the elections and immediately before the formation of the joint authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you can see from this document, Mr. Vukovic is sending an amended proposal of candidates for leadership positions. And here he goes on to enumerate the names of people, regardless of whether they were members of the party or not. And I'm sure you will remember and you will agree that the person listed under number 1 was not a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what your question is. What are you asking me in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to enumerate the people. Let's see, number 1, we have that on the first page. But may we turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 2 of the Serbian and of the English as well, please, on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, just look at those names there. Do you remember, for example, that Mr. Kovas who was there on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party, the republican prosecutor was not a member of the party and Simo Kuraica was not. Skoko might have become a party member but was not one at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we have the last page displayed, please. And the last page in Serbian as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that your name is listed is there under number 17 and it says that you were working at Sarajevo RTV, that you were a lawyer, and that you were proposed to be assigned to responsible duties in the Presidency. Now, my question is this: Do you agree that many of the people from this list were people who were not, in fact, members of the Serbian Democratic Party? For example, number 3, Ranko Nikolic, used to be a minister in the communist era and that the cadres commission led by Mr. Dukic adopted this and that these people were put forward as candidates to hold positions in the leadership?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that this is the first time that I see this document. I don't know on the basis of what authority Vukovic could have proposed cadres in this fashion, and I never knew about this until today. Most of the personnel, the cadres, that exercised power and authority had nothing to do with the SDS. And I don't know today how those people were put forward bypassing the SDS organs because they weren't members, in fact, of the SDS. Now, as far as I'm concerned, nobody proposed me to any Presidency or anything like that, nobody put my name forward. So my answer would be yes, most of the Serbs in the BH government had nothing to do with the SDS and were proposed to the positions they held bypassing the SDS or, rather, not as members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that topic, Mr. Neskovic, as to what guided us to have people who weren't members of the SDS proposed and entrusted with important state functions, but now may we look at 65 ter document 18531, please. 18531 next, please, and it is the minutes from the 1st Session of the newly elected Executive Board of the SDS of BH held on the 31st of July, 1991. Can you see the document and that in paragraph 2 it says that Karadzic attended as well as Krunic, Neskovic, and others? And now at the bottom there, under number 1, it says in paragraph 1 that Karadzic proposed the election of the president of the Executive Board and then put forward the proposal of Mr. Rajko Dukic, put forward Mr. Rajko Dukic for the post. Dukic thanked him. Now, do you remember that Dukic had his own party and that he joined the Serbian Democratic Party when you did?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but if this draft translation is a full translation of the document, then I would ask that the English page be placed to correspond with the B/C/S. But if it's not, I think we need to know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a Prosecution-approved document. It's -- we do have the translation, N0301736. Or rather, we can hand it over to the Prosecution or put it on the overhead projector perhaps. It wasn't up to us to have an approved translation or not -- and to upload the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to get into a procedural wrangle. I think if we're going to use the document and it's possible to get the translation on screen, we should do so. That's all I'm asking at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger, that must be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I understand it can't come up on e-court, but it could come up on the ELMO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we don't need the English portion of the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, can you work that way, Dr. Karadzic? Is it coming up on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. We need to manipulate it a bit, but I'm sure we'll make our way. Can we look at the bottom of the page where it says Dukic expressed his gratitude but asked that somebody else be elected because he was already working. He had an enterprise in Vlasenica, so he was busy with other matters. And then we can turn to the second page both in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now on page 2 can you see that for his deputy, deputy of the president, Rajko Dukic put forward Mr. Radomir Neskovic, as it says there. And then in paragraph 2, or point 2, Dukic stressed that the Executive Board would have six commissions, for social affairs, for information, they're all listed there, for agriculture, forestry, and the water industry, and so on and so forth. And now at the bottom you see it says: "The members of the commission put forward so far are prominent experts in their individual fields." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that from the very beginning our criteria was that they be professionals occupying these posts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I apologise, but I have to say that the professionals were in the Serbian Democratic Party. According to this, it would appear that the party did not have any professionals and that they had to find professionals from outside the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But may we now turn to page 3 in the Serbian and the English can stay on the screen. That page of the English was fine on the screen. May we have the English back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the document's been uploaded to e-court. It may be easier to work that way. The Registrar is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, it has been. Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that stress here is laid on the fact that all these people and all this work must be conducted at a high professional level, and then Dukic went on to say that the party president from the previous year to the present day had not been remunerated for his expenses during the performs of his functions and so on and so forth. Do you remember that portion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your interview with the Defence you stressed, on page 12 of the Serbian version and page 11 of the English, that a problem loomed in the party, the people felt tricked. They had given a great contribution to the electoral victory and then suddenly other people appeared who had been in the League of Communists previously and that that's how the leading positions were filled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D3487 displayed, please, on e-court next. Page 12 of the Serbian and it's 11 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree looking at this document here that -- well, the first paragraph about the disagreements and after the People's Assembly -- well, do you agree that the elections in 1990 brought not only a change in the regime but a change in the system of socialist self management, or rather, socialist self management became a multi-party democratic system; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that I was anxious and worried that the cadres of the Serbian Democratic Party -- or rather, let me ask you this first. Do you agree that the personnel and most of the cadres of the Serbian Democratic Party had been dissidents for many years beforehand, that is to say, they were far removed from the exercise of government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The SDS had thousands of cadres. It did have a number of dissidents but it also had people who had nothing to do with power and authority. But it also had members, many members who were professionals and knew how to govern. So it was a very well-educated and professional party base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that there was the danger that after 40 years of suffering, the Serbian Democratic Party, or rather, its membership in one way or another might wish to take its revenge on the people who had ruled them for 40 years and that there could have been a new division among the Serb people except that now all the democrats would be the ones who would laud it, if I can put it that way, over the communists?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have two questions there. First of all, I don't accept that there would have been revanchism of the SDS over members of the party who had lost power. Now, your second question. That is true, you did strive and advocate the fact that the Serb people should be one whole and not be divided into Chetniks and partisans within that body of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, and you have it towards the bottom of the page, that I made a proposal immediately after the elections that an expert government be established and not a party government in order to reduce tensions which were already burgeoning in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the other two parties did not accept that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- you proposed the formation of an expert government, but when it came to realisation, when ministers were appointed, we saw that it nothing to do with experts in the government. They were ministers from the list of the BH League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that as opposed to the SDS, the SDA brought to the leadership functions party people exclusively?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and so did the HDZ and that's why the elections were held, so that the party people could take over power and authority on the basis of the votes. And if power and authority were to remain with the cadres of the former party, then there would have been no need for elections, they would have been senseless. So yes, they did appoint their cadres to positions of power and authority, whereas the SDS did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page, please. The Serbian is 13 straddling 14, and the English is 12 straddling 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember correctly that the only minister of the cabinet of the joint Bosnia-Herzegovina from SDS was late Velibor Ostojic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you stressed that I had proposed that a new basic organisation be introduced, local board instead of municipal board, and you spoke about that today. And in the interview you confirmed that the main organisation of the SDS was a local one and that people were directly elected by the membership. And then representatives were delegated upwards. Do you agree that people were elected upwards and requests were made from lower levels to upper levels?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: For 1991 and the party elections and the electoral Assembly, that's correct; but I'm not sure about 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, 14 in Serbian and 13 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When my advisor asked you to what extent the SDS was organised, how well it was organised and how long it took to make it fully operative, you answered it took about a year and it became well defined and operative on the 12th July 1991. And then you said that it was defined vertically and horizontally on an absolutely democratic basis and that one could not be part of the SDS organisation without having the support of a local board, except in the case of certain experts. And then you said that in democratic terms the party was defined very broadly, but in 1991 it had no power or authority in the republic, it had no influence on the authorities. And then you said, "We didn't have a single man in the Presidency of Bosnia at lower levels." And you describe a situation where the Serbs in power are one team and Serbs in SDS a different team which lasted all the way up to 1996. I'd like to ask you: Do you remember that in 1990, I did not run for a single state position and I wanted in that way to set an example for other SDS members, that they should only serve their own people, not strive for power; is that correct, that I did not run for any positions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier today Mr. Tieger asked you about traitors. Do you agree that that referred to betraying decisions that had already been made because it was a multi-party system. It was not allowed for anyone in the SDS to carry out policies of another party and it did not apply to decision-making but only the implementations of -- implementation of decisions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The guiding principle in the SDS was democratic centralism. There was democracy in decision-making and the charting of policies, but in the implementation of those policies it was centralism. What was wrong with the SDS was factions inside organisations, that was not tolerated. Any influence by other parties on the SDS was not tolerated, and the leadership was to be separated from basic organisations. That's the way centralism operated and people who would depart from this would be criticised and sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the only high-ranking person expelled from the SDS was late Vladimir Srebrov who wanted to turn Young Bosna, the youth organisation of the SDS, into an iron fist of the SDS and the board expelled him after long debates without any proposal for my part. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe he even became Vice-President of the SDS in Skenderija and he was expelled because of his positions about Young Bosna as some sort of party guard that was not very well liked as an idea. So he was expelled and another person who was expelled was Milakovic from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were no other expulsions perhaps all the way until 1996, when some members established their own parties?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were no expulsions because the culpability of a particular member had to be proven by his local organisation. Nobody could be expelled without eliciting the opinion of their local organisation. So there were no expulsions, as far as I remember, while I was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 16 in Serbian, later 17, and in English that would be 15 and 16 -- sorry, 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Serbian, towards the bottom, you say: "I don't remember. I told you --" It says: "I don't remember we were removed by any decision of Karadzic's, but as far as the government and Presidency and the MUP, many people expected to get into power after the elections, but Radovan persistently avoided implicating the SDS in state authorities and he kept old staff in their positions." You say Mandic had nothing to do with the SDS, Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in Serbian. It's not the right page in English. It should be 14 and later 15. 15 towards the bottom in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you keep on enumerating. Do you recall that not a single chief of a regional centre of the MUP was a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, no. In fact, it was the rule. Former members of the League of Communists were appointed to all positions, not members of the SDS, and that continued later on during the war in Republika Srpska, the same policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you answer here: "I heard that discussion while testifying in the Krajisnik case, where you said that the leadership of the SDS was one thing and the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs another thing." And you said these were two separate things; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then on page -- Serbian page -- Zepinic officials -- and then you say when Bosnia-Herzegovina broke up, when Republika Srpska was created, Karadzic did not allow the SDS to exert influence on the government or to appoint ministers because they would have appointed themselves, which is logical. We would have sat down and divided positions among us and we would nominate ourselves as parties tend to do; right? And I was a hindrance to the complete take-over of power by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you implemented systematically one certain policy. At the republican level in Bosnia and Herzegovina or Republika Srpska it was your policy not to allow SDS members to take executive power, and through your influence you placed former members of the League of Communists in those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that I made sure that they had left the League of Communists and they were nonparty personalities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what your hopes were. All I know is that the SDS never came into executive power at the republic level.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in English. In Serbian I would like to see page 19 now and page 17 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My advisor asked you: "What was the relationship between Dr. Karadzic and the leading politicians in the Krajinas?" And you said: "It didn't work so well. People from the Krajinas were rather independent. They were not afraid, like Kupresanin, they did not fear Karadzic, they opposed him, freely criticised him and put forward their own positions. There was no submission in it. The Krajinas displayed a great political independence." Do you remember that even before the elections in 1990 there was a kind of competition between Banja Luka and Sarajevo, and the entire Krajina had a constant chip on the shoulder that everything is being given or taken over by Sarajevo and they wanted some balance restored?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The Banja Luka region always displayed resistance to Sarajevo, be it Bosniak, Serb, or Croat sources. It always aspired to greater independence and they always put forward arguments that Banja Luka, a very big city, ranked 18 in terms of development. In any case, they did not like it at all that Banja Luka, such a major centre, ranked 18 in terms of development.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that it was mainly, first and foremost, an economic issue?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was an economic issue. They had a strong resistance to centralism then as they have now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we keep page 19 in Serbian and have page 18 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My advisor asks you: "Generally speaking, did Karadzic allow you to carry on with the democratic process and debates?" And you say: "We have to be precise. Throughout this period, as far as party relations within the party are concerned, Karadzic was a great democrat. Everyone was free to debate, express their opinions, there was no dictatorship, no oppression. Everything was very democratic and free in communication within the party."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was great democracy in decision-making and the work of the Executive Board, but centralism ruled in the implementation of policies already charted. There was democracy in decision-making, but centralism and hierarchy in the implementation of these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can keep these pages on the screen. You say: "Within the party and debates in the Main Board, the party was democratic, there was no dictatorship. The party did not suffer from authority. For instance, the authority of Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic and Koljevic was not felt in the Main Board. Krajisnik did not even ask for the floor. He couldn't say, You know, I'm the president of the Assembly, let me tell you this and I'll go. We couldn't care less that you are the president of the Assembly. You are a member just as we are. So Radovan was not really burdened with authority."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Krajisnik, Plavsic, and Koljevic never even took the floor at the Main Board meetings. They were just present there and they did not play a big role in the Main Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 30225 is the next document I would like to see in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 30225 is an intercept of a conversation between you, Miskovic, Srdic, and myself. This discussion took place on 10 September 1991. You were already in your position of vice-president of the Executive Board, and you were at that time obviously in the field. 10 September 1991, that's it. Karadzic, Neskovic, Miskovic, and Srdic from Prijedor. We can see, and you remember, that there was a big problem with the local authorities in Prijedor. Municipal deputies from the SDS became renegades from the party because they refused to work along with the leadership of the SDS. There was a man Milakovic there who ended up as a criminal. Do you remember there was chaos in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember about conflicts within the municipal board in Prijedor and the various factions, but I don't know about the work of the deputies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to the second page now, please, or rather, page 2 of the Serbian and 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that, right up until the end, we did not succeed in dealing with the situation of the party in Prijedor and that it was terra incognita, a completely unknown situation there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. But there were always two factions fighting for supremacy within the municipal board and the situation was never completely resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 2 of the Serbian and 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my reply. I say: "Please tell us. Those who don't wish to respect party policy and wage party policy but are engaged in their own private policies." And you say: "Yes." And then on page 4 of the Serbian and 6 of the English, Karadzic says: "But wait a moment. Let me tell you. Listen to me please. Do as Neskovic has proposed, but tell the deputies that they're on our list and not us on their list and they have to behave properly towards the party that brought them into power and you do as follows." Do you remember all that? Do you remember that that was the position we took, that the deputies that once they were elected for a particular party programme and for a particular party, then it was up to them to promote that programme? Let's now look at page 6 of the Serbian and 8 of the English. Do you agree with what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the deputies should promote party policy because it was the party that elected them. But don't forget that I put forward my own proposals, although I can't remember the details of my proposals for a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you can see that I supported those proposals; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And you were very angry and you swore a lot. You were extremely angry at Srdja and Miskovic and the situation in Prijedor in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it says on page 6 of the Serbian and 8 of the English: "Yes, but last time there was Srdjan and Savanovic and they didn't act as we had agreed. They did not do as we agreed." And then page 8 of the Serbian and 11 of the English, Srdjo is speaking and he says: "I won't allow anybody to disabuse you because somebody said who is Karadzic? What does he want? Who listens to him? We'll do what we want to do. He can't impose his will on us. He can go and say things like that in Sarajevo," and so on. Now, do you agree that this confirms that the party gave great leeway and freedom to activities and that to a large extent it had been decentralised in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this conflict in Prijedor surpassed and went beyond the usual measures of political pluralism and democracy. This was a clash between two clans and probably in the background you had personal interests, large personal interests. So the conflict was very serious and this surpassed democracy. It was a clash between two factions in the municipal board in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when it says "Who cares about Karadzic? Let him do what he wants in Sarajevo," is that resistance towards the centre which the whole of the Krajina displayed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's just Srdja Srdic and his thirst for power, and he didn't want to leave his post and did everything he could to remain performing the duty he performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document, but just as an MFI, for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, a couple of matters. First of all, I don't think that's necessary. I believe that's on the associated exhibited list. Secondly, when -- again, I hate to raise it again, when Dr. Karadzic says "this is me speaking," I don't think it's appropriate for MFI. I think it's been authenticated and he can't present it on the one hand for such and then call for an MFI process. Also it involves this witness who has simultaneously authenticated the exhibits. For any number of reasons I can't imagine that marking it for identification is appropriate rather than admitting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, this does appear to be one of those intercepts whose -- the authenticity and accuracy of which you appear to not only accept but to put forward; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if I could answer that. You frequently remind Dr. Karadzic that he's not giving evidence during this portion of the case. I think we have the right to put the Prosecution to its proof with respect to the reliability of intercepts and they've chosen to delay that until some time later in the trial when they call the appropriate witnesses. So we're not in a position -- we should be in a position where we are able to challenge the reliability of intercepts and at the same time protect ourselves in the sense that if intercepts are found to be reliable and found to be admissible, we get the benefit of those which are favourable to our case. So, otherwise we would have to sit there and wait and do nothing with intercepts and then call all these people back to try to use the intercepts if you decided that the Prosecution has established that they are reliable and admissible. So I don't think that's a good procedure. In this way we are able to challenge the intercepts and at the same time preserve our ability to have the information before the Chamber in an efficient way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The reality is that in the end I think it won't matter that -- but this -- clearly the Defence's position, that is, proffering a particular document as reliable to make the point it's attempting to make in examination, is a factor to be considered in its admissibility and has nothing to do with whether or not Dr. Karadzic is testifying. This is what the Defence is doing by way of that particular document. This is a Defence position on it. In any event, it's going to be a factor to be considered one way or another, and I think that we continue to see that these intercepts are indeed reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson, it's not a question, of course, of Dr. Karadzic giving evidence; it's a question of whether or not he accepts the authenticity of a document, which is entirely another matter. But although it's -- it seems to me to be Delphic as far as logic is concerned, we will MFI this simply for the point of consistency. As Mr. Tieger accurately observes, at the end of the day it probably won't make any difference. While I'm speaking, we're sitting until 1345 today. What I propose is that we take a break now for 20 minutes, we recommence at 10.40, and for planning ahead, the second break at 11.45 until 12.15. So we'll rise now until 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What has happened with the intercept? What's its number? What's the number? May I be given some information about that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's MFI P2571.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I have 1D3487 again, please, ID 3487, which is the Defence interview with you. 1D3478 is the number. And may we turn to page 21 of the Serbian and 19 of the English. You say here that at the Main Board, from 1991, there was a Deputies Club which adopted attitudes and didn't have to report back to the Main Board, and then you go on to say that the party couldn't adopt positions and issue instructions to the deputies as to how they were to vote. And given the circumstances, it was the Deputies Club which assumed all the power and authority. Now, do you agree that this was a great problem for the SDS, in view of the fact that the other parties had full control of their membership and deputies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the other parties had control over their deputies. I really can't say. I don't know. But what I do know is that the SDS Deputies Club was a constituent organ which passed all constituent acts and documents which lay the grounds for Republika Srpska and that it didn't have to receive orders from the Serbian Democratic Party or answer to them. They worked autonomously. It was a centre of power in its own right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I put it to you that in the Western democracies parties have a deputy or a whip, if I can put it that way, following the work of the deputies to see whether they're acting in line with party policies, did the SDS have this whip given to them by God, so to speak, in the Assembly and otherwise in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I have to say that the Deputies Club of the SDS was not an ordinary Deputies Club. It made up the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it passed constituent documents. So the party didn't have this whip ordained by God or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm sure you know the famous proverb about our lack of co-operation which says: You have two Serbs and three parties. Do you agree that in Republika Srpska these deputies that came from the SDS, 72 from the SDS, and the rest from the reformist parties, the communists, and so on, that they behaved as if they represented 83 parties and not one; that is to say that they were completely independent and autonomous in the decision-making process and very often stood up to -- very often the SDS deputies would oppose each other?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did oppose certain opinions and say what they thought with respect to policy, but it's a constitutional act to pass documents and the SDS deputies were unanimous when documents and acts were passed. They exercised consensus and they had another one from the -- 73 from the SPO and the other deputies from the Assembly who came from other parties, they had different -- took different positions and later on formed their independent Deputies Club within the Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now turn to page 26 of the Serbian which is 24 of the English of this same document. You say here that the SDS -- that the role of the SDS was strengthened when it came to organising a plebiscite because the deputies could not organise a plebiscite without the SDS, of course. Have you found that passage? And the party played a major role in organising the plebiscite and then its role after the plebiscite went downhill again, whereas the SDS Deputies Club took on a central role once again, a central role as a central political body or body for political decisions. Do you agree that the party transferred all its power and authority to its representatives in the state organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The party didn't do this. It was the state organs who transferred the power. They did not -- they were not duty-bound to report back to the Serbian Democratic Party at all. The Serbian Democratic Party would not have transferred this to the executive organs in the positions of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So people from the party were angry at me because of that in a way, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 29 of the Serbian and 27 of the English displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here, and we'll find it, Karadzic said, I think, in one of his speeches that decisions were being made at the Deputies Club. He appointed all sorts of experts there without any connections with the SDS so the SDS began to fade away, stop all its activities. And then came the shocking decision of the government of the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina led by Djeric -- it should be with an R, Djeric. Do you agree, Branko Djeric; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, the SDS in July 1992, or rather, June 1992, in a special way was banned. The decision banned all political organisations and their activities, but being the only one, the only party, the SDS was banned. And that's how it was banned and this caused a further rift in the SDS. Do you agree that the government of Republika Srpska under the leadership of Professor Djeric was completely independent and autonomous in its work and that this came at its proposal without having the party interfere in its work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. The government exceeded its authority on this point. It banned the political organisation from operating one which was in power and which had formed the government in question, and this was unheard of in politics, that the government which was formed on the basis of a political party should ban that political party from operating. And I think that the government overstepped its authority on this point and had no right to ban the political party that was in power from operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that, at that point, in order to alleviate the situation I issued an order that the operation of the SDS should not be banned but rather put on ice?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They would never have agreed to something like that. We were banned from operating by the government in a perfidious way, and the order applied to all political organisations and banning all political organisations from operating but there was just us. The government overstepped its authority on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that until such time as the SDS was reactivated in February 1994, a couple of parties were set up, such as the socialist party, the radical party, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian radicals of Vojislav Seselj were set up. The socialist party, as a branch of Slobodan Milosevic's party, was set up as well. We regarded as -- not as a contribution to the multi-party system, but rather as an attempt at reinforcing those parties which had their head offices in Belgrade while undermining the influence of the party in power. That was my understanding of it. So yes, these two parties were formed during the war which makes the entire situation contradictory. On the one hand, the government banned the ruling political party from operating whilst, on the other hand, allowing parties from Belgrade, such as the radicals and socialists, to set up their local branches over here. So I understood it as a policy directed against the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 22217, a 65 ter document, which is the transcript from the Krajisnik case. In e-court it's page 166. So page 166 in e-court of 65 ter 22217. Can it be enlarged?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read out your answer from, say, line 7: [In English] "It depended on the people in leadership positions in the municipalities; some had a tendency to act for independently. In the case of the Municipal Board of Banja Luka, that board did not really feel it had to respect party discipline. There were other such Municipal Boards ... but the party structure prescribed in the statute was somewhat disturbed by the unlimited possibility that representatives of Municipal Boards had to go and see Mr. Karadzic, to speak to him in person ... Karadzic might tacitly authorise them to act in a different way ..." and so on. [Interpretation] Do you agree -- do you recall the jokes Branko told me the other day without saying that it was Branko Mikulic, in fact. Do you agree there was a possibility for manipulations, that people would present themselves as having received the backing of a prominent personality without it, in fact, being so?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of a specific case, but I do accept that there could have been instances where people tried to manipulate situations in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 30481, 30481, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an intercept, page 2, is that right? It's a conversation between myself and Ante Jovanovic, who says: "Believe me when I tell you that I wrote and we have made an agreement with the personnel of ours from the MUP. I'm short of 22 policemen of Serbian nationality and they need to be transferred to me. And now, for instance, I'm telling them that constantly, If you come tomorrow I won't have a police force, I won't have a police force, and they haven't helped me at all. And I say, Well, don't mention that to me anymore. I don't know whether they will come or not ..." et cetera. He goes on to say: "Well, it's not about that. I mentioned you because I wanted them to provide me with a police force." Will you agree with me that this is one of the instances where Mr. Jovanovic is trying to achieve something for his own purposes by referring to my name as an authority in the case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about this. Let me tell you that the MUP itself was far removed from the party. Except for Mico Stanisic who was a member of the party, there were mostly non-party individuals working there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to 1D3487, 1D3487, page 50/51 in Serbian and 47 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My advisor asks you as follows: "Since the Prosecution also seem to insist that the SDS is one and the same thing with Republika Srpska, what is your comment on that?" You say: "It's not the same thing." What do you have to say about this, that the SDS was removed from the government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that at the level of the executive branch on the local regional level, and even later on on the national level, the SDS was not part of the government and SDS does not equal the executive government. As for the municipalities themselves, well, that's not the same thing. The SDS did participate in the power-sharing with the SDA and HDZ after the elections. So the situations on the local and regional levels differed greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in both Serbian and English. We can keep the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page you say in this interview: "The situation with the government and the SDS that I still am at a loss to understand persists to this day. Not a single government, Djeric's, Lukic's, Kozic's," I suppose you will agree with me that it's Kozic and not Kojic, "was ever proposed to the Main and the Executive Boards and personnel affairs, nor did anybody ever ask these organs about anything. The SDS could not even be in the government in Pale ..." And that's what you said; is it right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were then asked: "Was it not the case that the SDS operated through the Assembly of Republika Srpska? Who was in that Assembly?" And you say: "Well, the Assembly is just one body where indeed there were SDS deputies." Can we turn to the next page in English, please. "However, the SDS did not issue any orders to them and they constituted a centre of power in its own right which acted autonomously." In your next answer you say that they were an autonomous centre and 98 per cent of them were appointed by the SDS but they did not answer to the SDS at all. They were completely out of SDS's control. Therefore, this confirms that the deputies operated autonomously. They were not controlled by the party and were able to act upon their own conscience.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the way I see the Assembly is the -- the SDS is the constituent party representing the Serbian people who laid the grounds for Republika Srpska. So they -- the deputies of the SDS were an authority in their own right, and when it came to passing these basic decisions, they acted unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to correct, the transcript should read: "Well, yes," because you said, "Well, yes, the way I see ..." et cetera. Do you agree with me that you said "Well, yes"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that the deputies were independent, they were an autonomous constituent body of the Serbian movement and did not take orders from the SDS. They were unanimous to a high degree. Yes, they did not receive orders from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the 65 ter 22217, page 16 in e-court, the transcript we looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From line 2 your answer: [In English] "At the top of the party, President Karadzic, who pursued his policies, tried to ensure that legal principles were followed in the broad party organs when he took decisions, so he tried to act at the top, but a lot of initiatives were taken at the municipal level." [Interpretation] And then line 8: [In English] "There was a lot of democracy until a decision was taken, and when a decision was taken, then the usual party hierarchy was implemented." [Interpretation] Line 13: [In English] "So I would call this a principle of democratic centralism." [Interpretation] This is what you stated in the trial against Mr. Krajisnik. Was that your position and was that the case at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 151 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, to the extent possible, may I suggest for clarity of the record and ease of reference that 65 ter 22217 and other -- be referred to as P2568 which is the exhibit number it now bears. And to the extent we can do that for other exhibits that had been admitted, I think that would be to everyone's benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That seems to be logical.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 10 you say: [In English] "Between March 1991 and the 31st of July, 1991, I would have had to visit at least something in the range of between 25 or 30 municipalities." [Interpretation] And then at page 152, page 152, line 20: [In English] "No. Up until the 31st of July, it had to do with the pre-electoral activities within municipal organisations, electoral matters. After the 31st of July, we were talking about other activities, routine work of Municipal Boards and their functioning and overcoming problems and disagreements between fractions within those Municipal Boards." [Interpretation] And another passage on page 161, please, from line 13. [In English] "When you made your visits to the municipalities, as you've described, in 1991, you were not carrying to the municipality instructions from the leadership of the SDS, were you?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] "I wasn't carrying any particular kind of instructions. The statute was quite sufficient for me, the statute that was in force. To be frank, I acted in a fairly independent manner. It was possible for me to decide on how to deal with certain problems; I could do this in an independent manner. But I had not been issued any precise tasks." [Interpretation] Do you agree that you stated this, namely, that basically it worked that way, the statute was the fundamental document that was acted upon, and you had great liberty in finding ways to apply the statute?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the statute was the fundamental document binding upon everyone. In view of the fact that the statute introduced a novelty, that the local board was the basic organisation, diminishing the influence of municipal authorities, the municipalities reacted by disapproval because they were no longer the basic organisation. Yes, I did act in this way and my role was mainly the role of a mediator based on the current statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there could have been no greater decentralisation of the party than by identifying the local board as the main organisation in the socio-political community?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think this is about decentralisation. This is an original concept of organising party politics, where the basic organ of the party is the one that is the closest to the grass roots, because the Serbian Democratic Party was organised as a centralised party in terms of organisation without the middle regional level. There was no regional level. So all the party activity took place between the local board and the highest level. The activity developed up the chain, that's how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to another subject, the subject of regionalisation, to the extent that you knew about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2568 is the document I would like to call up. I'm sorry, that's the interview. I'm calling 1D3487, 1D3487.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's your interview with the Defence. Here you answer, when you say at the Main Board you have to say at which session, and so on and so forth. And then you say: "The idea of regionalisation originated in Banja Luka. The people who advocated the Autonomous Region of Krajina were the ones who came up with the idea of regionalisation, and that's the only region which was in fact established. All the other regions existed only on paper. They just proclaimed their regions and nothing else. That means you can't lump them all together." I'd like to ask you this about regionalisation. Even before the elections and forever in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the regional distribution often criticised but all the critique came mainly from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't quite understand the question. But as far as Bosnia and Herzegovina as a federal unit was concerned, it had strong institutions at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it had a strong position in municipalities so that municipalities had their own Assemblies. The house of municipalities and deputies were elected from these Assemblies. There was a strong position of municipalities but no regions, no middle level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the situation we found in place when we won the elections, the council of municipalities and the citizens' council in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that demands for regionalisation were very old, much older than the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it would be more correct to say that demands for regionalisation were much older than the regionalisation itself. The regionalisation occurred later. The first stage was decentralisation in the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 15 in Serbian -- sorry, this was page 9 in Serbian and page 8 in English. We did not show them. They accompanied this first answer. Now I'd like page 15 in Serbian and page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You speak about the organisation, this is your first answer on this page. You say: "Regionalisation was an official topic between Karadzic, Izetbegovic, and Kljuic, it was no secret, no taboo, it was much discussed." And a bit further down: "Alija insisted on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina while we were against. And on the other hand, Serbs insisted the Bosnia and Herzegovina be decentralised." And yet further down: There was the regionalisation that created municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina. The SDS created Bosnian Krajina. The reason why the first region came into being is that, in summer 1991 or earlier, the war began in Croatia, so people were mobilised there and went to war in Croatia, whereas the war was not felt in Sarajevo. Here the war atmosphere prevailed much earlier and representatives of the municipalities, Serbs, created the Autonomous Region of Krajina without asking for anyone's permission, Karadzic's or Kljuic's. And then because of the war in Croatia, this region already had its legislative authorities, the budget, the army, the police, et cetera. Following the example, other regions started proclaiming their own regions, north Bosnia, Majevica, et cetera, but they remained regions only on paper. They were never institutionalised; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 18561 in e-court. The 2nd Session of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party which you attended. It says Dukic was president of the Executive Board, Draskovic vice-president. I attended, Buha, Dutina, Ilic, et cetera. It's English page 2, listing the people present. Can we now go to Serbian page 4, English page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 6, it was ascertained that the platform, meaning the platform on independence; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think it was the platform on the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia dated -- no, sorry. I don't know which platform it was. I thought it was the one of 14 October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was finalised on the 14th of October, but it was always the case that platforms had to be ratified by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know really. I never attended sessions of the Assembly. This is probably about a platform that was being prepared for enactment, but I'm not sure which specific platform is meant here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to slow down for the interpreters. Item 6: "It was ascertained that the platform, constitution, and referendum were unacceptable because they were, in fact, three very cunningly calculated blows to the Serbian people. We are emphatically against any imposition of solutions because there are solutions acceptable to all peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then item 8, English page 6, it says: "It was pointed out that the inter-party agreement on the implementation of personnel policy was not being carried out, especially in the MUP but also in other organs of state administration."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Energetic work must be done in this area because the functioning of certain state organs and services in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been compromised."
