Do you remember that the Serbian Democratic Party had to fight for the positions that belonged to it according to the inter-party agreement, but the implementation of that agreement was sabotaged and the other two partners marginalised the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, the SDS was removed from personnel policy. From the very beginning, it did not make any decisions about personnel. Personnel policy was charted outside the Main Board. I believe you did the main work on that together with Rajko Dukic. Now, what you agreed with the SDA and the HDZ, which positions you had agreed upon, I don't know. In any case, personnel policy was not dealt with by the Executive Board so I don't have any information about the agreements between you, Kljujic, and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D3487 again, the interview, page 18 Serbian, 16 in English. Let's just wait for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the top, my advisor asks you about the establishment of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. "At that time Karadzic was just president of the party, but how did Karadzic and the leadership of the SDS view the establishment of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?" And you answer: "There was no unanimous position ..." and a bit further down you say: "... but personally, I saw it as an exertion of influence on the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, pressure on Muslims and Croats to accept the regionalisation as a precondition for the Serbs to accept some sort of confederation." Do you agree that in the end it all resulted in our acceptance that Bosnia could be independent, on the condition that it be restructured from inside?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood, but I'll try to clarify this. Throughout 1991, the interest, the main interest of the Serbs was to remain within Yugoslavia. The Serbs did not accept an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for this regionalisation, it took three different forms. One was the regionalisation that you negotiated with Izetbegovic; the second, the regionalisation implemented by Krajina and other regions; and the third was the one done by the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thus, the Serbs, and you in the leadership, refused the option of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina all the way up to that autumn. But after the peace conference on Yugoslavia and the Badinter Commission, when it became clear that Yugoslavia was breaking up, you accepted that Bosnia become independent, on the condition that it be transformed and decentralised in some form. Now, which form, it was not quite clear. That's how I saw these events, and I have to stress also that with Izetbegovic, sometime after October 1991, you had intensive negotiations about resolving the political crisis. But from October onwards there was all-out conflict between the three parties and every party went its own way. So the conflict between the leaders of the parties dates back to October. We can say that the leadership of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina sometime in end 1991/early 1992 was prepared to accept the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but only on the condition that its internal structure be changed, decentralised, federalised, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, staying with that document, may we have page 27 of the Serbian and 25 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In response to a question of whether you, as member of the Main Board or the Executive Board, ever learnt of some plan for part of Serb territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be separated, cut off, your answer was no. Is that your answer today, secede a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, your answer was no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I can just give a yes or no answer. But what -- or, rather, I cannot. But the Serb position was that we are going to stay within the remaining state, same state, which was Yugoslavia, and the territories where we are in the majority we will keep within Yugoslavia. Now those who wish to secede from Yugoslavia, the Bosniaks and Croats, that is, can secede but without taking away our territories. And in that way, we wanted to shift the responsibility for the crisis onto the Bosniaks and Croats in this way, which is to say we support the existing state and remain within that state. Anybody wishing to secede from that state, let them go, and this kind of policy was legitimate up until the Badinter Commission, which interpreted the fact that Yugoslavia was in dissolution, that it no longer existed and so on. Otherwise, the Serb question in Bosnia and Herzegovina was -- well, the Yugoslav question was dominant rather than Serb question, less energy was invested to reach an agreement with the other two nations about their own position within Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then we faced a wall at the beginning of 1992, when Yugoslavia left us hanging and created the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, defined its western borders, and the Serbs from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were left outside that territory. Unfortunately, we in Bosnia-Herzegovina were more Yugoslavs than the leadership of Yugoslavia. We strove for Yugoslavia more than Yugoslavia's leadership did. So all I want to say is that there was this necessary change of circumstance. One is the interpretation given by the Badinter Commission. Reality was different after the interpretation provided by the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that with the existence of Yugoslavia all the Serbs and Croats and Muslims lived in a single state?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 29 of the Serbian and 27 of the English, staying with that same document. Page 27, please, and then we'll be moving on to page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked here about a meeting held on the 19th of December at the Holiday Inn hotel, and you said that yes, you attended the meeting. And then what was the meeting about was the next question and your answer was: "I don't know ..." et cetera. There were members of the Main Board, the Executive Board, deputies, municipal leaders, various others -- other people, chauffeurs, escorts, there were more than 200 people. Let's say there were 45 people in the Main Board, 15 or 16 in the Executive Board, and so on. So there was no particular agenda and what was to be discussed was the situation in general and the overall -- and overall Serbian documents, the plebiscite, Yugoslavia, Bosnia, and the Muslim documents, those of Krajina, and so on. There was no agenda, no particular agenda. Now, do you remember that on the 19th of December, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina unauthorised, without an Assembly decision and without convening the Assembly, asked the European community to recognise the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that in those dramatic moments this meeting was convened. That is the backdrop?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the BH government did make that request, but I don't know that it was this particular date and I don't know that this meeting was convened because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's stay with page 28 of the English, and may I have page 30 in the Serbian displayed, please. You described at one point in the interview the way in which decisions were taken and documents made of the Serbian document -- SDS, that they were prepared by these experts, that there was an extensive discussion, the decision would be adopted, it would receive a number, a stamp, a signature, and would come out with -- as an official document with a reference number and everything else. Is that how the SDS passed its documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very serious. There was a separate legal commission - I think I was a member of it - and all the documents were written and passed in a very serious manner with all the attending procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now talking about this Variant A and B, the document that was distributed at the meeting and you say: "However, what is debatable in the document is that it says 'Crisis Staff of the SDS,' which is incorrect because the Crisis Staff of the SDS and Main Board never existed. At least I never knew of it as a legal organ. I attended I think 99 per cent of the Main and the Executive Board. The Crisis Staff never existed." And then a little further down you go on to say: "The document never got into the SDS organs nor was it filed anywhere. It wasn't discussed neither as a draft or as a thesis, nothing. It just appeared just like that, out of the blue. Radovan brought it with him." And then still further down you go on to say: "He was sitting at the corner of the desk and handing it out to people to read and return, but he didn't say, 'This is an order, you have to do this.' There were quite a few contradictions. The document said strictly confidential, or some sort of secret, and yet it was distributed amongst 200 people. It said that the SDS had prepared the document. It wasn't prepared, in fact, by the SDS. It also said that the Crisis Staff was established but the Crisis Staff or a Crisis Staff didn't exist." Now let's look at how you describe the way in which -- the way in which SDS documents were prepared, staying with that page -- or rather, we've already established that. You said that it was done in a very serious, highly responsible way. And it says here in the SDS -- so anyway, do you agree with what you said about the structuring and formation of SDS documents, and that this document, A and B, was -- did in no way correspond to that serious procedure and was not engendered in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The A and B document is a contradictory document in all its details and elements. What I know about it is that it wasn't written in the SDS, in the legal commission or the Executive Board or Main Board. The Main Board and Executive Boards of the SDS did not pass it as one of their documents and the Crisis Staff of the SDS -- well, I don't know that it ever existed. I don't think it did. And it's not a document which came into being along regular procedure practiced by the SDS party. It came into being in a fashion in which I'm not aware of, and you promoted it -- and elsewhere, and you promoted it in December or made it public at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now turn to page 31 in Serbian and 29 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is what it says: "I later learnt a secret document -- but this B, I wasn't clear on what that was. The B -- that B wasn't clear to me. It said that when you were a minority, when you were threatened, when your physical survival was threatened, you had the right to oppose and even use arms to protect the lives of the group, and I didn't understand what the need was for emergency acting in a situation where a majority in the municipality -- when any decision could be adopted in a regular procedure or an emergency procedure." Now, does this indicate the fact that somebody proposed this to the Serbian Democratic Party, somebody who was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the document is quite incorrect. Now, if somebody put forward a document, then they should have written "proposal" and signed the document proposed by whom, so that then the SDS could discuss the document. We have here the erroneous writing of the Crisis Staff of the SDS and strictly confidential. We have a series of contradictory elements and details precisely stipulated, but we don't have the writer of the document or the group of people who wrote the document, which I consider to be completely erroneous procedure. If something is proposed, you have to write "proposal" and you have to say who is tabling the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that already in December -- or rather, let me put it this way. Do you remember that at the beginning the JNA and the pensioned officers as old-time communist cadres, that they were very wary of the SDS, the SDA, and HDZ as national parties, they didn't approve of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they viewed the HDZ as being enemies, hostile, because there was the conflict with Croatia. The SDA was viewed as an enemy and they viewed the SDS as a necessary evil, a party that they were opposed to, but since there was no other party then it was a necessary evil, so to speak. And as we can see from the document, we don't have the interest of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina dominate here. What dominated was Yugoslavia's -- the interests of Yugoslavia, and including the overall Serb component in preserving Yugoslavia as a state. And in fact, Serb interests have been equated to the Yugoslav interest here quite erroneously. So if the Yugoslav interest has been jeopardised, then automatically the Serb interest was jeopardised in BH, which was quite incorrect. So the writers of this document see the interests of the JNA and Yugoslavia as their focal point, and the Serbs -- they're just using the Serbs here as a means to realise that end. I don't understand this document as being in the Serb interest. I understand it as being in the Yugoslav interest and put forward in a very incorrect way, quite wrongly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we're going to take the second break now. Thank you. And we'll resume again at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that it was anonymously distributed, and therefore incorrect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said anonymously written, quite, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this answer you indicated that this A/B variant is much clearer now because this was a minority that could be threatened and activities in circumstances of being under threat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to call up in e-court 65 ter 16731, 16731.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from minutes of a meeting of the local boards of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. This is your region; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And we can look at the second paragraph which states: "It is a fact that many members of the Municipal Board have fallen into the embrace of the government and that they are serving the government. We know very well that the formation of the Crisis Staff in these difficult times was done with the best of intentions and with the aim of safe-guarding the interests of the Serbian people." Do you agree that the Crisis Staffs on the Serb side were established only in February or March or April 1992 while the Muslim side had Crisis Staffs practically throughout the whole of 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know of the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo. That is what I am familiar with. I don't know when the others formed their Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the purpose of the Crisis Staff was exclusively the protection of the people?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that we could take it like that because if protection of the people depended on some Crisis Staff or other, then that -- people would have a very difficult time of it. I don't think so. I think that the position of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina depended on the decisions of the Assembly, the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and its actions, that these were the constituent acts, not those of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it states here at this meeting of your local boards that the forming of the Crisis Staff was done with the best of intentions and with the aim of safe-guarding the interests of the Serbian people -- well, perhaps this would be a better question. Do you differentiate between a party Crisis Staff and a municipal party -- Crisis Staff, a Crisis Staff of a party as an informative body which reports back on political positions and the municipal Crisis Staff as an institution of the local government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The party Crisis Staff of the -- of Novo Sarajevo is something that I don't know much about. I know about the municipal staff, but that staff included cadres from the party. This one specific here is the one in Vrace and I think that the background for this meeting was quite different, which was not actually stated in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree that the first idea was for the Crisis Staff to serve the people in organising their defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the participants at the meeting were not thinking about the Crisis Staff. There was a struggle for power between the two factions in the Novo Sarajevo municipality. And in the Crisis Staff one side criticised the other, that it wasn't working enough on the formation of the Crisis Staff, it wasn't working enough on the protection of the Serbian people, it wasn't active enough in the plebiscite. So these questions or issues served as a pretext for one faction to settle accounts with another in the Crisis Staff. So I think this is the background for this meeting. It is something that would continue and culminate in late February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this was not a rare occurrence, it was not something that happened only in this municipality, it happened in other places as well, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only speak of the municipalities where I did go. There were instances of a struggle for power, especially in rich populated municipalities where power was important. So within the boards there was a struggle for power. Here, as far as I know, there was a struggle for power exclusively between Serbs who were in power and those who were not in elected bodies in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this -- we would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 6609.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes from a joint meeting of the Main Staff, the Executive Board, and the Political Council of the SDS of the BiH held on the 11th of March, 1992. Do you remember that at that point in time there was a conference underway under the auspices of Lord Carrington and Mr. Cutileiro which will result in the so-called Lisbon Agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I think this was in the same hall where the meeting of the 19th of December was held, and I remember this because I think I spoke at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the third paragraph in the Serbian. I think we will find it in the English as well. It was indicated -- this is actually the third paragraph in the English. "Furthermore, it has been stated that in the field ..." and then it lists Trebinje, Banja Luka, Sipovo, Ugljevik, Novo Sarajevo, Doboj, Ozren, et cetera. There are serious problems which are the result of inactivity and non-execution of the agreed policy. And then the following paragraph states: "There is a need for an urgent discussion regarding the standpoint on the Yugoslav national army as a very sensitive issue. The first and main thing is one's own army with its own insignia, especially as both Croats and Muslims have introduced their own army and their insignia in their own areas." First of all, do you agree that up until that time, even before this was something that was stated at the conference, do you agree that the Croats and the Muslims already had their own armed formations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that information, although I don't have any evidence of it because I didn't see those armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second, do you remember that as part of the Lisbon plan, the Lisbon Agreement or Cutileiro's plan, the idea was for all the constitutive parts to have their own national guards? Other than the police they were also supposed to have their own militia or national guards?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Cutileiro Plan or the Lisbon Agreement are well known, but they were never actually implemented, they never went into force. They were signed but the implementation was abandoned. They were never implemented. So it's hard to say had it been implemented what the -- what form the implementation would have taken, how everything would have been done. But this case -- this agreement was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we will come to that. All I wanted to ask was whether this part of the minutes speaks about us having more harm than benefit from the Yugoslav People's Army. While the others were forming their own armies, we were supporting an army that we could not actually command.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav People's Army as a multi-ethnic entity ended up in Serbian hands. Muslims, Croats -- Croats, Bosnians, and Slovenians left the army leaving only Serbs there. The SDS had a positive attitude towards manning the ranks of the army. The Serbs responded to the call-up, to the regular and reserve forces. So that army actually became a predominantly Serbian army. Their conduct at the beginning of the war and who had what use or harm from it is something that I can speak about only as it relates to Novo Sarajevo. Anything else would be speculation and I would not want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That will be tendered -- exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D3487 again, the interview, 1D3487. Page 42 in the Serbian and page 39 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the document we know as the Variant A and B and you confirmed was distributed without any particular recommendations by the parties, that it should be adhered to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the A and B variant document was distributed, people read it, and they were obliged to return it to you. The document was not discussed, it was not put to the vote, it was not amended or augmented. It was simply promoted there and people understood it in different ways, some as an obligation, some less so, some were confused, and so on. In any event, at the meeting we did not have time to read the document thoroughly. We just were briefly informed about it, did not have time to read all of the elements. Only later during the war I managed to get a copy and I read it from beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is a charge in the indictment which states that Mr. Cizmovic was the person responsible on my behalf for the implementation of that document in the field. From January 1992 onwards, did Mr. Cizmovic come to your municipality? And my advisor did ask you that on this page of the interview, and you said that he did not. Did anyone come to monitor the application of the Variant A and B document and was there any insistence from the party on the implementation of that document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No one came to Novo Sarajevo. As for the role of Mr. Jovan Cizmovic, I think that he was some kind of co-ordinator for inter-regional co-operation at the regional level, the Serbian autonomous provinces or regions that were proclaimed. As for the document itself, later when reading it we did see a passage where the implementation of the document was possible only with your personal approval, and in the document you are indicated as the person who decides if the document would be implemented and how it would be implemented. As for Novo Sarajevo, there were no contacts or any visits from the government to that area. We were left to our own devices to do as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P2568, please. P2568 and page 73 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are being asked here by Judge Hanoteau: [In English] "Those who were there and those who received the document, were they in a position to make any comments ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And your answer was: [In English] "Well, they did have the possibility; it wasn't forbidden. They could have taken the floor, and they could have made the comments they wanted to make. But given the atmosphere in the Assembly, given the emotions, given the atmosphere, it was perhaps not conducive ..." and so on. [Interpretation] And then the Judge asks you further: [In English] "So if I understand you correctly, the emotional atmosphere that prevailed was one of fear." [Interpretation] And can we look at the following page, please, in the English. Your answer: [In English] "Well, you could put it that way. One could say that there was fear, fear of being out-voted, the fear of Bosniak and Croat dominance." [Interpretation] And can we now look at page 170 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART ASKS YOU
utterances.text: [In English] "Mr. Neskovic, I'll put this to you, then: Are you saying that apart from the Variant A and B instructions, as you put it, that you were not yourself aware of any instructions, directions, or guide-lines given to municipalities from the higher levels of the party in late 1991 or early 1992?" [Interpretation] Your answer is no, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the party did not give out any instructions because it was the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was issuing series of enactments from 22nd October until 19 January 1992, and those were the basic documents, the fundamental documents, on the basis of which everyone acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to 1D3487. 1D3487, page 32 in Serbian and 33 English. 30 in English and 32 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked first: "Who conceived Crisis Staffs in municipalities in the first place? Was that ever discussed in the organs of the party?" And your answer is: "I don't think so. As far as I remember from the transcripts, no. There was great diversity. Already at that time you had an institutionalised Krajina that established Crisis Staffs at the level of Krajina. In other places, you did not have Crisis Staffs and there were none at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina." When you were asked why was a Crisis Staff set up in your municipality, you answer: "The first Crisis Staffs were established based on some instruction from the government, that was in Djurovic's locality." And when you were asked which date, you said: "It was early April, perhaps the 10th of April. That Crisis Staff fell apart, it had held only one meeting, and in that Crisis Staff I was in charge of office space." And a bit further down: "The Crisis Staff stopped working at that point after only one meeting. Djurovic went to Belgrade." Is it indeed your position as you stated it in this document, and was it indeed the case that everyone did as they saw fit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe according to the instructions from the government Djurovic formed a Crisis Staff. He was chairman of the Executive Board in Novo Sarajevo municipality. He had great reservations about Variant A and B. He didn't want to apply it. He tried to avoid it. He thought that he could attain his objectives within the legal framework in the municipality. He formed this Crisis Staff that fell apart after just one meeting, and he himself left Grbavica and went to Belgrade. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D407. I hope we can see the English. This is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the instructions for the work of Crisis Staffs in municipalities issued by the government of the Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it the instruction to which you made reference earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: It's from 1990, but I never read it even at the time and didn't care for it. We took a negative attitude towards instructions from the government. I don't know the contents but I know of its existence and I know that it was on its basis that Crisis Staffs were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "The Crisis Staff takes over all the prerogatives and functions of Municipal Assemblies in war time whenever Assemblies are unable to convene ..." And then in point 2 we see who makes up the Crisis Staff. 3, its task is to defend territories and defend the population. Number 4, number 9 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- the Crisis Staff is duty-bound to create conditions for the work of international humanitarian organisations. Number 9, the Crisis Staff is duty-bound to create proper conditions for the work of international peacekeeping and humanitarian organisations and to enable unhindered passage of convoys with humanitarian aid ..." et cetera. Number 10: "Treat non-combatants and the wounded humanely in keeping with the ICRC, also prisoners of war, and act in every way in accordance with the laws of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina." Regardless of the fact that you have not read this instruction, did you basically act in keeping with these provisions in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For instance, did you co-ordinate the work of the authorities to protect the territory and defend the population?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else do it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the police and the Territorial Defence and later the army had to take care of that. The Crisis Staff that I presided over created independently of this instruction our own work. We thought the position of the government to be very inappropriate. The government is shifting its own responsibility to municipalities. Municipalities are supposed to do their own work, and the government did not even tour the localities or offer any assistance. The way I see it, the government shifted the burden of the crisis to municipalities and it sort of loses power. The Crisis Staff that I set up with Sarovic was not based on this instruction. We did not care for government's instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the government had no great influence on municipalities and the municipalities did not get any assistance from the government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking for Novo Sarajevo, we did not get any assistance. But the government did have influence because they had all the funds and resources. The municipalities did not have their own resources and did not have the funding to deal with any issues. This inadequate policy remained in place throughout the war. The whole burden of the war was shifted onto municipalities. I believe the government was not working properly and put a greater burden on municipalities than they were able to withstand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that your grudge against the government is perhaps justified because the government was close to you, but do you agree that at this time towards the end of April, the government could not have any good communication or even physical connection with more remote municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. The government was able to have communication if they wanted to have it. I stand by my position that the government acted very irresponsibly towards municipalities, shifting the burden of the war onto them. Those people in Pale could have known if they wanted to, they could have helped if they had wanted to. They had all the power, all the money, all the resources. It was in their hands, it was up to them. The government could have received information if it had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is in evidence. Can we go back to the interview, 1D3487.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, do you agree that, from the beginning, everyone hoped that it was not going to be a war, just a crisis, a short-lived one, and that's the reason why Crisis Staffs were formed first and the Presidencies of municipalities were set up only later?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not say so. It would be logical to create Crisis Staffs before the war. It's only when the crisis really sets in that the Crisis Staffs are supposed to be established. We were all hoping at that time that the war would not escalate to that extent and that the JNA and the Presidency of the republic with all their meetings will do everything to avoid the war. And I believe you and Izetbegovic indeed made efforts to find a peaceful solution; however, the problems surpassed your capacities. In order to get a good outcome, a more positive attitude was required from the Croatian President Tudjman and the Serbian President Milosevic because the crisis could not be resolved peacefully without their involvement. We were all hoping that there would finally be some agreement between the presidents of the various republics. However, those hopes were dashed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 34 in Serbian and 32 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here already from the 12th of May, when the army was established, Mladic said he did not recognise the Crisis Staffs. Do you recall that it turned out the Crisis Staffs were unable to influence the army, they were not recognised, and that is one of the reasons why they ceased to be?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's about something else. The government very cunningly shifted the burden of the war onto municipalities and Crisis Staffs, and then in the end of May they found that the Crisis Staffs were not doing a good job, that it was not a good solution for managing municipalities. Then the Crisis Staffs were disbanded, and then the Presidency was established. It lasted only ten days. And then the decision was changed again to set up war commissions. So it was all very haphazard and random. It was unclear what the authorities at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina were going to do about the authorities in municipalities. There were several solutions, Crisis Staffs, Presidency, and war commissions. And as far as Mladic is concerned and the army, he had great reservations about this new SDS. They favoured the League of Communists and they were very sorry that this party fell through in the elections, and then they accepted the SDS as a necessary evil, hoping all the time that other parties would come into power, such as the Serbian radicals, and that they would get greater powers and a better position in Belgrade. So generally speaking, high-ranking officers did not like the SDS very much as the main, national party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 34 and I believe English page 32 or it's the same page, you say -- now about Grbavica, that's before the bolded "Krasno." And now Grbavica, this Crisis Staff, it was all on paper. You're making believe that there is a Crisis Staff, but you are completely impotent. Was that really your belief, that it was something on paper without any powers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: There were two different periods. When Grbavica was not under the control of the Serbian army and the Crisis Staff was in Vrace. What I said here refers to that period. You have great obligations and facing great expectations from the population, but you can't do anything. The situation is completely different in May when the Serbian army took Grbavica over, the situation changed for the better. They found a large number of well-organised people in Grbavica, prepared to defend themselves. There were proper resources and proper capacity to work. So these are two distinct periods, before the take-over of Grbavica and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the take-over of Grbavica you say the people organised themselves. Now, could the Crisis Staff guide these processes, prevent any crimes from being committed, or influence the events in any way before the army took control of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have done so in the municipalities where it had the resources. If you had warehouses, depots, medicines, fuel, and other such resources that you can use for the people, you could. But if you don't have those resources, then you couldn't do anything. And secondly, you could wield an influence if you were superior above the -- to the military units and so on. If you were a commander, you could effect security; but if you weren't in charge in any way, then you couldn't wield any influence on the security issues. So for you to be able to wield an influence, you needed resources, backup.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 33 in Serbian and 31 in English, staying with the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your answer there in the middle, "Well, I personally," that sentence -- no. But this Crisis Staff, you say, dissolved and nobody from the government or the Assembly came, nobody from the commission came or Presidency, and the people were left to fend for themselves because of the so-called officials. "Only Miljko Sarovic and I stayed on in the area and so did Prijic, and I talked to Miljko, Prijic, about what we were to do, and then at Vrace we single-handedly formed a Crisis Staff according to our own -- by our own accord without asking the government for instructions." Is that the right description? You said you were left to fend for yourselves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we move on to page 35 of the Serbian and 32 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a brief exchange between you and my advisor. From the 10th of April to the 10th of May, you were in the Crisis Staff, that's what the person says. Then you say "yes." Who did you report to in that period? Your answer: "Nobody." The question was: "Did you have telephone lines?" Your answer: "There were none." "Q. All right. Did anybody from the leadership visit you up to the 10th of May? "A. Nobody." And a little further down the page or on the next page in English: "We did that all on our own without consulting any authority at Pale." And a little further down again, you say: "Except for Mucibabic, no other high-ranking official came to ask us how we were. I might have gone to Pale on one occasion to ask for some resources from the municipality for coffins, but the people from the government really left us in the lurch. They never even asked about us nor did we ask about them" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm at a loss to understand why in the course of recounting this lengthy answer that has to do with contact -- the -- there is skipping over the portion about someone who did come. So if that's going to be read into the record and stand on that basis, it needs to be read out in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you can see Mr. Tieger's point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will be tendering the entire document, but what I'm just doing now is, for the purposes of cross-examination, making a short selection. Otherwise, we're not going to skip over everything, we're going to tender the whole document in due course, but we're trying to save time during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's appreciated, Dr. Karadzic, but as long as the point that Mr. Tieger has raised is plain, that if you're going to have information in, then the whole of the information needs to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not Milomir Vuckovic, it's Mucibabic. I did mention Mucibabic. I just skipped the upper part. So Mucibabic did come and I said that. And Mucibabic wasn't an official. He came as some sort of commissioner with instructions, bearing instructions. But as I say, we'll place the whole document at your disposal. May we have 36 in Serbian now, please, and 34 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you like to say something more? Do you consider this interview to be complete? Would you like to add anything on the topic that we're discussing, that is to say, the visits to Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you have in mind. Milomir Mucibabic was a sort of commissioner from the government, but otherwise, nobody came from the government. And the atmosphere was a very negative one, negative towards the government and towards you too because it was considered that you should have stayed on in Sarajevo, remained there and shared the destiny of the rest of the population and not have gone to Pale. And the prevailing opinion was that the population was left in the lurch and that that was why there was this negative attitude towards the authorities in Pale. Otherwise, the rest is as I have stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you're asked, staying with that page: "Did you have any contacts with other Crisis Staff in Serbian Sarajevo municipalities?" Your answer was: "No, we could not have. I just went once to attend a meeting because we had to take the roundabout route. We were physically cut off from Ilidza, Hadzici, Ilijas, and so on. So you would need a whole day to get there. So we went to Pale. Nobody invited us nor did we go, actually. I just went once or twice. Once there was an army uprising and a civilian rebellion." And then you go on to describe how you presented a sharply worded petition and that: "Radovan said nothing, said not a word," that is to say, I didn't oppose anything, "nor did Krajisnik, but it was rather unpleasant because we wrote all sorts of things against the leadership and we aimed more at the government which had taken up," and so on and so forth. So as the Crisis Staff and the leadership of the municipality, you had to solve problems such as coffins for those who had been killed and so on and so forth, and that's why you went to Pale, whereas you had absolutely no contact with the government and the authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I went to the government when it was in -- put up in the Kikinda building. That's the first time I went. I don't think the Army of Republika Srpska had still been established. There was a Territorial Defence and a brigade down there of the Territorial Defence, that's all there was because of the war, and people were killed. And so it was necessary to procure coffins for those unfortunate people, and I was rather surprised because I thought it was the Ministry of Defence that took care of that, including coffins. But I think I went to see -- well, one of the ministers in Kikinda anyway and I resolved the problem of these coffins. I think that they were manufactured at Sokolac. So that was my first contact with the government, and I didn't understand why the Crisis Staff now which had a role in the Municipal Assembly had to deal with coffins for the dead. I thought that there was some military institution that would deal with things like that, but unfortunately, we confirmed that the government had shifted the burden to the municipalities and it was the municipalities that had to take care of everything, including coffins for the soldiers killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 37 in Serbian and 34 in English now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is where you describe the argument over the petition and the rigorous stand you took vis-à-vis the leadership. Page 34 of the English said: "We had a serious argument on account of the petition. We put serious accusations on the leaders that they were going to sell out Sarajevo, betray us, sell us out that it wouldn't be ours. We had a fierce disagreement about them giving up the airport. That was one item. The other item was that we wanted to know what the borders were. People were asking and we wanted to prevent deaths" and so on and so forth. Do you stand by that position expressed there, that the local authorities had a lot of criticism to make of the government and the central organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Not only the authorities, but the population as well. The problems that the authorities had went way beyond what they were capable of doing. And it was especially difficult because there were no leaders and officials and higher organs to give you any guide-lines. You were left to fend for yourself, to do what you could given the circumstances, which was a very difficult position to be in. And I remain by the stand that the government did very little to help the municipality there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have P2568, please. I think that's the right number. Or first of all D885, please. D885 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a report of yours to the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 5th of June, 1992. Do you recognise this report and written that way with a reference number and the date and as set out, is that how reports are generally written?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my report and I think I wrote it in just one copy. I think you were to have it photocopied. I haven't got a copy of it myself, so I haven't had a chance to read it through again. But yes, that is the report I sent to you on the 5th of June, 1992, and I think I wrote it in Bistrica at Mount Jahorina and I think I handed you the document personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are stating here that an Executive Board has been formed as an executive organ of the municipality and that you were taking care of the population, that all refugees from the occupied territories and people who were left homeless had been taken care of in the areas of Tilava, Lukavica, and so on. Then you go on to speak about food supplies, local communes made lists of civilians which included their first and last names, and food supplies amounting to 50 per cent of peace time supplies were distributed to those on the lists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say the population, food supplies for the population, did that refer to the Serbian population or to the population in general regardless of nationality or religion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The entire population. I think we had two food kitchens open. At Grbavica we had people in charge of distributing that food and we tried to have it honestly distributed as far as possible. We had food shortages to begin with, but then the French army stepped in, UNPROFOR, and they brought in vast quantities of food to Grbavica and throughout the war they fed the population of Grbavica. So the population of Grbavica can be grateful to the French UNPROFOR which helped the population, and then the food that they brought to us on a daily basis we further distributed. So that was the French -- the assistance provided by the French section of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to speak of food supplies for the army. Now, the next section, health care and medical corps. You say a health centre with five surgeries were formed and civilians were treated as well as everybody else, and during combat action it functioned as a military hospital. So you were left without a health centre and you had to establish a new one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we were left without a health centre; however, this was a relatively easy problem to resolve because there were surgeries at Grbavica, well staffed, so they just continued working and we didn't have to invest any great efforts. Quite simply, the medical staff continued doing their work, the same staff that worked before the war in the surgeries. And at Grbavica there was a very well-known surgery with very professional staff and had all the resources necessary to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that it provided assistance to civilians and all people alike, did that refer to the Muslims and Croats as well living in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both in terms of food and medical assistance. I think there was a lady doctor at Grbavica. She was a Bosniak. Now, as far as food was concerned, we had to make lists of people requiring meals in public kitchens and I think that the French would control this, control -- look at the lists to see if they were multi-ethnic or if they were just mono-ethnic. But as I say, the medical assistance did apply to all citizens, regardless of nationality or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under point 6 you talk about the attitude towards Muslims and Croats and you say: "Meetings are frequently held, especially in Grbavica, of citizens of all nationalities and we pick a person in charge about all entries made, a head for every building responsible for the situation in his building, and we informed the Muslims that they would be safe if they were militarily neutral towards us. And so far the situation has been good. We visited the nunnery in Gornji Kovaci ci and discussed co-operation, loyalty, and the nuns' safety." Now, my first question is this: Do you agree or do you know that the selection of a head for every building was in keeping with the Law on All National Defence -- All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second, do you agree that it was a good solution, that is to say, if some were -- someone were to commit a crime, a Muslim were to commit a crime, that the police was allowed to do their work without holding rallies or something?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these heads were not appointed for that reason, but they were appointed for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw a footage -- we saw footage of this convent in Kovacici. Were they Catholic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was at Gornji Kovacici, the convent there, and they were nuns who had been there for a long time and then left later on. They were Croat nuns, Catholics. Yes, it was difficult for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this was a good example of how we expected the municipal authority to function and that in the eyes of the leadership your -- their respect for you grew?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. But I had a video-tape from the joint meetings that we held with the Bosniaks and Croats, and I think that this was a good example of how one should behave given war-time circumstances. Unfortunately, it didn't last long because later on, during 1992, for instance, the situation radically changed. So I'm very sorry that this did not go on for longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to say what you were doing at your level in the municipality, was it in keeping with what we wanted to be done or did you elicit only my critique?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I was doing it of my own accord, not expecting praise or criticism. I did not have a care for what the government in Pale was doing because I had too much on my plate and I wasn't worried about whether -- whatever leadership agreed or disagreed. No, I did not actually receive any criticism from the leadership over this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see again 2568, P2568, page 129 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From line 8 the question: [In English] "Now, the last sentence in the first paragraph of item 6 of the June 5th report, as I mentioned earlier, says, 'Secretly, the police applied the usual procedure to people who were engaged in military activities against us.' "If you know, what was the usual -- what was the procedure that the police was applying to Muslims and Croats?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] "That meant that since all the Muslims had been asked to surrender their weapons on a voluntary basis, and they did that, the Commander Major Petkovic said, 'Since you have done that, the army won't search your flats. We'll have a Muslim at each entrance who will be in charge of that entrance and will ensure that everyone is there every night ..." [Interpretation] And a bit further down, line 20: [In English] "... and this concerned the Muslims who didn't want to surrender their weapons and they acted against the Army of Republika Srpska. They provoked action over the radio, or there was sniper fire because they believed that those who were carrying a weapon were no longer citizens; they were soldiers. And if any inhabitants noticed such a person, they should go to the civilian police and report on the fact, and then further police procedures would be implemented. And it meant that if anyone noticed such a person in their building, they should be reported." [Interpretation] That is the sort of thing you did not say at meetings in order not to upset the citizens. This is how the protection in Grbavica worked; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult. This was some sort of preventive confidence. The war made a confusion between civilians and the military. It was very hard to distinguish in the city who is civilian and who is combatant, because you can see a civilian in the street, he goes back into his house, takes up a weapon, and he is no longer a civilian. Then he leaves his rifle behind and becomes a civilian again. It was very hard to distinguish in the city. And we were trying to warn Croats and Bosniaks that if they do not attack the Army of Republika Srpska, they have the same rights as any other citizens. But if they act against the army, even by radio or passing on information, they would lose their status of civilians and they would be investigated by the police. So if anyone notices such a person, they are required to report it to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same document, page 113, here you say line 2: [In English] "Initially the situation was fairly good, given the wartime conditions. But sometime in the second half of 1992 - perhaps that was in July or in August - certain groups started to expel the Muslims and made them flee to the other side of Miljacka. In Grbavica, there -- we have to distinguish between Grbavica I, where our Crisis Staff was located and where the civilian authorities were located, and there was also Grbavica II, which resembled Stalingrad; it was a military position ... and I think that the Muslims were expelled in droves from Grbavica II ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 115 now, please. [In English] "As far as Grbavica I is concerned, as far as I can remember, this did not go on for days and days. I believe that this only occurred on one day, but it was a terrible day, an ugly day, and these very ugly things happened. On that day, individuals were expelled and made to cross over to the other side ..." [Interpretation] And so on. [In English] "There was a commander, major, called Dragan Petkovic. He also treated them very correctly because he lived there ..." and so on and so on. [Interpretation] These things that happened on this day, were they done by an organised unit under somebody's control or was it some other elements?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that date in August, but on that day I ran to the apartment of Olja Varagic, and there was my friend there also from radio and television, and I wanted to stay there for one day to help if somebody comes to the door. So I don't know who was doing this, but it was totally unnecessary. It was criminal to treat innocent citizens from Grbavica like this and to expel them to the other side, to mistreat them, to rob them. The military police, the military prosecutor's office should have taken this situation under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that was certainly against the will of your civilian authorities in Grbavica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The army never asked us for anything. We did not even have contact with them. We were even kidnapped once by the army. They put us into their vehicles and took us to the front line. So we did not even dare approach the army, let alone had any influence on them. We had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you confirm here that Major Dragan Petkovic treated Muslims and Croats fairly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Petkovic treated Muslims fairly, Croats and Serbs fairly, making no distinction. But I believe sometime later in the summer, Petkovic was transferred. He didn't stay there. I think he was sent to Zvornik. So I can say that within his own field of authority, Dragan Petkovic was a decent person, treated everyone fairly, and I believe Muslims and Croats who still live in Grbavica can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This man whom you visited in order to give him protection was your work colleague, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we used to work together at Radio Television Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D3487 again, page 39 Serbian, 36 English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, what was the source of that danger to your friend whom you went to protect? Was it the police or the army or neither?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: There were armed people in uniform all over the place. You couldn't know to which institution, to which unit they belonged. There was no way of knowing. You could not tell who was a member of the army and who was a paramilitary. Both wore uniforms and both carried weapons. Only the military police was able to do that, but they were pretty idle, unfortunately. As for this man Djipa, Batko was dangerous to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer. The interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry, can the witness please repeat the last part of your last answer. The interpreters were unable to understand it for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orhan Djipa, his life was in jeopardy from the person called Veselin Vlahovic, known as Batko. Because on one occasion Batko had arrested Orhan Djipa and it was only Simo Sipcic's quick reaction, that man was a military policeman, that saved Djipa's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now you see on this page my advisor asked you: "Was there talk about any incidents or crimes against Muslims at that meeting?" You say: "No. Radovan kept his silence, whereas Moma tried to iron it out. He didn't say anything specific. He just said we shouldn't be afraid, there was a leadership, that they are thinking about Sarajevo." Was it the occasion when you filed a petition against the leadership, and in this answer you confirm that there was no information, no reports, about crimes against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: At that meeting concerning the petition in Kikinda attended by you, Krajisnik, General Tolimir, General Mladic, and four or five of us from municipality Novo Sarajevo, and Prstojevic from Ilidza municipality, the main topic was what would happen with Sarajevo and the status of Sarajevo, that was the main topic, and we didn't discuss anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 42 in Serbian, 39 in English. We have these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say: "A system remained in Grbavica I controlled by the army under the command of General Markovic --" sorry, that's Petkovic. He's now major-general. "He calmed the situation down as much as possible. They did not allow searches or expulsions, and the people started approaching them slowly as people you can trust, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. Petkovic had an apartment there before in Banja Luka Street." In other words, are you trying to say -- sorry. "Petkovic used to have an apartment in Banjalucka Street, so people knew him there and the officers were rather tolerant and even the police who were there were rather tolerant, except some people who were trying to create problems." In other words, are you trying to say that citizens were able to approach the regular forces, the army and the police, and they would be met with understanding and given protection?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only talk about a short period in the early days of the war when Major Petkovic was there. He did inspire confidence. As for others, the Muslims and Croats from Grbavica treated the Serbian authorities very decently and tried to self-organise themselves to contribute to finding solutions to problems. They tried to work together with others and they did not even protest against the work obligation. Some even joined the army. But the only thing they couldn't tolerate was to be humiliated or mistreated. That was a period in the early days. However, when Petkovic, and later Novakovic, left, the situation changed for the worse. Now, to what extent the military police, the military security, the state security, the civilian population and the military prosecutor's office and the military courts were understanding of the problems experienced by Muslims and Croats, I don't know. Only Muslims from Grbavica can tell you that. All I know is that in Novo Sarajevo and in Grbavica the organs of security had a major presence, the military and state security. There were two police forces, military and civilian, plus the command of the army, and even, I believe, in the summer of 1992 a military prosecutor's office and the military court were established. So citizens had somewhere to go. Now, whether these institutions were equally open to all of the citizens, I don't know. You would have to ask Bosnians and Croats to what extent they had access to these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Pofalici are a neighbourhood in your municipality that remained under the control of the BH army, whereas it was a majority Serbian or exclusively Serbian neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning Pofalici was not under the control of the BH army, at least not at of it. One part was under the control of the Serbian Territorial Defence and then there started fighting between the Serbian Territorial Defence and the BH army. And Pofalici then came under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the 14th and 15th of May, the civilian population were slaughtered in Pofalici where several dozens, if not hundreds, of Serbs lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: We have heard terrible testimony of people who had managed to escape. We weren't able to see it for ourselves. We haven't got concrete proof because we were quite a long way away from the area, but we can conclude that something -- we were able to conclude that something terrible had happened in Pofalici on the basis of eye-witness accounts of people who managed to escape to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Pofalici are across the river from Grbavica, the other side of the river and the main road; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: They're opposite the town and much further away, not only on the opposite bank of the river but on the opposite side of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean the hilly area?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this event with the suffering of the Serbs in Pofalici, did it upset the situation and did it undo the peace that you were able to reach at Grbavica and the security situation regarding the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite certainly it had a negative effect. Now, how far and to what extent, I wouldn't like to speculate. I can't speculate on the consequences of that particular occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 42 in Serbian and 39 -- ah, we've got those pages on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page and then we'll turn to the next page. You were asked: "In that period, during this period, while everything was fine, did you have contacts with Dr. Karadzic?" And you ask: "In Grbavica?" And the answer is: "Yes. You had no contacts with him at all?" And your answer is: "No, we had no contact whether Grbavica was liberated or not -- whether Grbavica should be liberated or not. And we didn't ask him from the beginning, nor did they ask us." And now we come to another question. That's right, next page, fine. That's fine. "Was he informed of the events that took place in this municipality or not?" That was the question you were asked. And the answer is: "The first time I informed him was in the letter I took, but I had no idea whether he was informed by other people or not -- or rather, whether he informed other people or not, I don't know." And then the next question is: "Did you inform him that everything was fine in the municipality, that everything was done in keeping with the regulations, the law?" And your answer is: "I informed him on the 5th of June for the first time. I hadn't informed him prior to that. I hadn't been informing him prior to that." "So, did you inform him that Muslims were still there and that everything was fine?" And your answer was: "Well, I informed him by giving him a list of all the elements, the details, and I had forgotten about that. When I saw that the Prosecution had this report of mine, they gave it to me for a few moments to refresh my memory. I didn't manage to read the whole document, but I think that I informed him in detail and as systematically as I could and knew." Now the next question is: "And what was his reaction?" And the answer is: "I don't know. He got it from me at that meeting and read it later. I think that he used it later and kept saying that the situation he had in Grbavica was all right. All that was going on down there, I think that his reaction was positive. Also Nikola Koljevic's reaction was positive and so was UNPROFOR's." Do you agree with what you said there in the interview? Do you stand by that now?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the events that I referred to in the report, yes. There was a positive reaction on the part of Nikola Koljevic, and you seem to be all right with it. Nikola Koljevic came and I think there was a positive reaction from UNPROFOR which supported the population throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I'm moving over to another area now, so-called Batko area, so perhaps this would be a good time to pause for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct, Dr. Karadzic, rather than start a new topic which would have to be stopped in two or three minutes' time. We will rise for today and recommence at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
